author: solution_review_rotation
audience: First-course linear algebra and single-variable calculus.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.B1 — Medium: Reserve space for a noisier sensor
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Recomputes measured-state lower clearance, held-input lower command, actuator membership, closest-input correction and worst terminal clearance; the unsafe reused command is checked explicitly.
exercises.replacement_html: The lower clearance is $0.35-0.08=0.27$. The bound becomes $u\ge0.1-0.27/0.5=-0.44$, within the actuator interval. Projection gives $u^\star=-0.44$, a correction of 0.36 metres per second. The terminal lower bound is $0.27+0.5(-0.44-0.1)=0$. Reusing $-0.5$ would instead give $-0.03$ and would not certify safety with the new error bound.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.B2 — Hard: A safe set can demand an unavailable actuator
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Solves actuator/safety intersection feasibility, checks equality and the zero-clearance impossibility, and uses the adverse velocity to explain why faster sampling cannot restore missing authority or indefinite safe operation.
exercises.replacement_html: Feasibility requires $0.1-2d_{\min}\le0$, so $d_{\min}\ge0.05$ metres. At 0.05, only $u=0$ at the upper actuator endpoint can satisfy the lower safety bound. At zero clearance the requirement is $u\ge0.1$, which is impossible. For any positive hold length, the worst disturbance immediately moves the state across the boundary when $u\le0$. A genuinely different backup capability is needed for indefinite operation. Any finite initial clearance eventually runs out under the constant worst disturbance when $u\le0$; reducing the operating region does not fix that. A finite-horizon operation could instead stop before its clearance is exhausted. A faster clock cannot create a missing control direction.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.B3 — Hard: Add the age of a measurement to its error budget
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Computes the integrated movement allowance and total current uncertainty, derives and projects onto the new action bound, evaluates the reused-command failure and states the delay-wide speed hypothesis.
exercises.replacement_html: Movement can change clearance by at most $0.9(0.1)=0.09$ metres, so the total present error bound is 0.14. The lower current clearance is $0.35-0.14=0.21$, giving $u\ge0.1-0.21/0.5=-0.32$. The nearest command is $-0.32$. Reusing $-0.5$ gives terminal lower bound $0.21+0.5(-0.6)=-0.09$. The delay calculation itself requires a valid speed bound throughout the delay; the current measurement cannot retroactively justify that assumption.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P1 — Easy: Read a barrier-defined safe set
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Solves the safe-set inequality and evaluates all three barrier values, including the included zero boundary and sign convention.
exercises.replacement_html: The safe set is $[-1,1]$, since $x^2\le1$ is equivalent to $|x|\le1$. The barrier values are $h(1/2)=3/4$, $h(1)=0$, and $h(2)=-3$. Thus $1/2$ is inside, $1$ is on the boundary and included, and $2$ is outside. The sign convention matters: this module uses nonnegative barrier values for safety.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P2 — Easy: Turn a barrier rate into an input bound
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Computes the derivative and barrier rate, rearranges the half-line and substitutes the given state. It interprets the interior allowance and boundary direction.
exercises.replacement_html: The condition is $\dot h+\alpha(h)=u+2x\ge0$, equivalently $u\ge-2x$. At $x=1/2$ this gives $u\ge-1$. The condition permits some negative velocity inside the safe set, but its allowed magnitude shrinks as $x$ approaches the boundary; at $x=0$ it requires $u\ge0$.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P3 — Easy: Repair a scalar nominal input
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Identifies the nearest feasible endpoint, computes the correction and objective, and explains why every larger feasible input costs more.
exercises.replacement_html: The feasible interval begins at $-1$, so the nearest feasible input to $-3$ is $u^\ast=-1$. The correction is $(-1)-(-3)=2$. Its objective is $\tfrac12(2)^2=2$. Any larger feasible input is farther from $-3$ and has a larger squared deviation. This is the simplest CBF-QP projection.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P4 — Easy: Check an inward-pointing vector field
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Checks both endpoint velocities and proves full trajectory containment by its explicit convex-combination representation.
exercises.replacement_html: At $0$, the velocity is $1\gt0$; at $2$, it is $-1\lt0$. Both point into the interval. In the explicit solution, $0\lt e^{-t}\le1$, so $x(t)=e^{-t}x_0+(1-e^{-t})1$ is a convex combination of the initial point and $1$. Both lie in $[0,2]$, hence the whole trajectory stays there. The smooth vector field also satisfies the regularity needed for the boundary criterion.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P5 — Medium: Project onto a two-input half-space
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Writes the signed Lagrangian, solves both stationarity equations and active constraint, checks all KKT conditions and objective, and invokes strict convexity for uniqueness.
exercises.replacement_html: The Lagrangian is $\tfrac12(u_1^2+u_2^2)+\mu(1-u_1-u_2)$ with $\mu\ge0$. Stationarity gives $u_1=u_2=\mu$. The zero input is infeasible, so the constraint is active: $2\mu=1$. Thus $\mu=1/2$, $u^\ast=(1/2,1/2)$ and objective $\tfrac12(1/4+1/4)=1/4$. Feasibility and complementary slackness hold; strict convexity makes this the unique optimum.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P6 — Medium: Check feasibility with actuator limits
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Derives the state-dependent half-line and intersects it with actual actuator limits at both states; the counterexample to all-set CBF feasibility is explicit.
exercises.replacement_html:
We need $u\ge1-x$. At $x=0.1$ this requires $u\ge0.9$, incompatible with $u\le0.2$: the feasible set is empty. At $x=2$, it requires $u\ge-1$, so every input in $[-0.2,0.2]$ passes.

The point $0.1$ is inside $C$ but has no admissible barrier input. Therefore this $h$ does not meet the CBF feasibility condition on all of $C$. Being inside the proposed safe set alone does not make the filter feasible; the controller needs sufficient input authority.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P7 — Medium: Include the worst-case disturbance
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Chooses the worst disturbance, derives the robust lower input and both numerical bounds, then checks equality under the adverse signal.
exercises.replacement_html: The worst-case condition is $u-0.3+x\ge0$, so $u\ge0.3-x$. At $x=0.2$, it requires $u\ge0.1$. Without the disturbance, the bound is only $u\ge-0.2$. Choosing $u=0.1$ at the worst disturbance gives $\dot h=-0.2=-h$, exactly the allowed lower rate. The robust correction accounts for the full adverse disturbance, rather than its mean.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P8 — Medium: Compute a high-order barrier condition
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Differentiates both auxiliary functions, computes the input condition and the valid first auxiliary value, then exhibits the negative initial auxiliary value at the second state.
exercises.replacement_html:
$\psi_1=v+p$ and $\psi_2=u+v+(v+p)=u+2v+p$. At $(1,-0.4)$, $\psi_1=0.6\ge0$ and $\psi_2=u+0.2$, so the condition is $u\ge-0.2$.

At $(0.1,-1)$, $h=0.1\ge0$ but $\psi_1=-0.9\lt0$. A high-order certificate requires starting in the intersection of the auxiliary nonnegative sets, not only in $\{p\ge0\}$. Enforcing the final input inequality does not remove that initial assumption.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P9 — Hard: Audit a zero-gradient boundary test
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Solves the boundary-start trajectory, computes the vanishing gradient, and identifies the exact missing regularity hypothesis with a regular defining-function comparison.
exercises.replacement_html:
Starting at $x_0=0$ gives $x(t)=-t$, which is outside $C$ for every $t\gt0$. Therefore $C$ is not invariant. Yet $h^\prime(x)=3x^2$ vanishes at the boundary, so $h^\prime(0)f(0)=0$ hides the outward motion.

The usual regular defining-function version of the boundary test assumes a nonzero gradient on the boundary. It fails here. Using the regular defining function $\widetilde h=x$ exposes the correct outward derivative $-1\lt0$. A vanishing gradient must not be treated as a safety certificate.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P10 — Hard: Compare continuous feedback with a held input
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Solves continuous and held-input trajectories separately, locates the crossing, and derives the exact inclusive holding-time range from the decreasing affine path.
exercises.replacement_html:
Continuous feedback gives $x(t)=e^{-t}\gt0$. The held input instead gives $x(t)=1-t$ during the first interval, so $x(1.5)=-0.5$ and it crosses the boundary at $t=1$.

The first held interval remains safe exactly when $0\le\Delta\le1$: the straight line is decreasing and its endpoint is nonnegative precisely under that condition. A continuous-time feedback proof does not automatically certify its sampled-and-held implementation; a sampling margin or discrete-time condition is needed.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P11 — Hard: Shift a feasible predictive backup plan
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Checks each original state/input, constructs the shifted tail plus terminal action, proves terminal invariance on the entire terminal interval and states model-agreement scope.
exercises.replacement_html:
The original states are $x_1=1-1/2=1/2$ and $x_2=1/2-1/4=1/4\in X_f$. Every state and input satisfies its bound. From $x_1$, use the shifted inputs $-1/4$ and $\kappa(1/4)=-1/4$. They produce $1/4$ and $0$, with the final point in $X_f$.

For every $x\in X_f$, $|\kappa(x)|\le1/4\le1/2$ and $x+\kappa(x)=0\in X_f$. This terminal invariance is what makes appending the controller valid. The argument assumes the predicted and realized first successor agree, or that model error is covered by robust constraints.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.P12 — Hard: Compute a shield and change the disturbance quantifier
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Identifies the complete winning set and all admissible inputs, then removes the disturbed action with a failure successor and explains the universal disturbance requirement.
exercises.replacement_html:
The winning safe set is $\{a,b\}$: from $a$, $L$ stays in it; from $b$, both original inputs stay in it. The shield therefore permits only $L$ at $a$, and $L,R$ at $b$. It rejects $R$ at $a$ because that directly enters $f$.

With the additional possible successor $f$ from $(b,R)$, the robust shield must remove $R$ at $b$ too. Although one successor is safe, the condition is “there exists an input such that every disturbance successor is safe”. Existence of a favorable disturbance is insufficient.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.1 — Forward invariance via the comparison lemma (proof)
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: All integrating-factor steps are shown; the nonlinear comparison ODE and monotonicity uniqueness are precisely applied from the teaching context. The measurable-feedback discussion distinguishes existence from safety of each existing absolutely continuous solution and explains the separate Filippov conditions.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Along the closed-loop solution set $\eta(t)=h(x(t))$; the CBF condition gives $\dot\eta\ge-\alpha_0\eta$. Multiply by $e^{\alpha_0 t}>0$: $\frac{d}{dt}\big(e^{\alpha_0 t}\eta(t)\big)=e^{\alpha_0 t}(\dot\eta+\alpha_0\eta)\ge 0$, so $e^{\alpha_0 t}\eta(t)\ge\eta(0)$, i.e. $h(x(t))\ge h(x_0)e^{-\alpha_0 t}$. If $x_0\in C$, then $h(x_0)\ge0$, so this lower bound is nonnegative and proves invariance. Every step is an equality or a multiplication by a positive factor, so no uniqueness argument is needed.

(b) For a general nonlinear $\alpha$, the same time-only exponential integrating factor does not cancel $\alpha(\eta)$: $\dot\eta\ge-\alpha(\eta)$ is a differential inequality whose "solution" is the comparison system $\dot y=-\alpha(y)$, $y(0)=\eta(0)$. The comparison lemma says $\eta(t)\ge y(t)$, but it needs unique solutions of the comparison ODE; $-\alpha$ is only continuous, and uniqueness comes from monotonicity ($-\alpha$ is non-increasing, a one-sided Lipschitz condition), which is the point Ames et al. 2017 make with the monotonicity uniqueness argument. Then $y(t)\ge 0$ because $y\equiv 0$ is a solution that cannot be crossed.

(c) Existence and uniqueness of solutions, not the inequality argument. With a discontinuous $u(x)$ the right-hand side of $\dot x=f+g\,u(x)$ may be discontinuous in $x$, so Carathéodory solutions need not exist (for $\dot x=-\operatorname{sgn}(x)$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(0):=1$ none starts at $0$) and need not be unique. Every solution that does exist is absolutely continuous, however, so $\eta=h\circ x$ is absolutely continuous ($h$ is $C^1$), the chain rule gives $\dot\eta=L_fh+L_gh\,u(x)\ge-\alpha_0\eta$ almost everywhere, and $e^{\alpha_0t}\eta$, being absolutely continuous with an a.e. nonnegative derivative, is non-decreasing. So the proof of (a) goes through for every such solution, and non-uniqueness is harmless because each solution satisfies the inequality. What is lost is the guarantee that the closed loop has a solution from every initial state, and a unique one that depends continuously on it. When $u$ is locally bounded, switching to Filippov solutions restores local existence but needs its own check that the barrier inequality holds for the convexified velocity set (here it does when $u$ is locally bounded: the inequality $\nabla h^\top\dot x\ge-\alpha_0h$ is affine in $\dot x$ and continuous in $x$, so it survives the limits and convex combinations of Filippov's construction). This is why the theorem assumes Lipschitz controllers and why Section 3 checks Lipschitz continuity of the QP solution. (Carathéodory and Filippov solutions, absolute continuity and "almost everywhere" are explained in the background note of Section 6.)

exercises.label: Exercise 10.2 — Closed form of a weighted CBF-QP (derivation)
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Complete weighted-QP KKT derivation with inactive/active cases, positive denominator, unique optimality and metric interpretation; every matrix/vector calculation in the example and the unweighted comparison is displayed.
exercises.replacement_html:
Lagrangian $\mathcal L=\tfrac12(u-u_{\mathrm{nom}})^\top H(u-u_{\mathrm{nom}})-\mu(a+b^\top u)$, $\mu\ge 0$. Stationarity: $H(u-u_{\mathrm{nom}})-\mu b=0\Rightarrow u=u_{\mathrm{nom}}+\mu H^{-1}b$. Complementary slackness: if $\psi:=a+b^\top u_{\mathrm{nom}}\ge 0$ then $\mu=0$; otherwise the constraint is active, $a+b^\top u_{\mathrm{nom}}+\mu\,b^\top H^{-1}b=0$, so $\mu=-\psi/(b^\top H^{-1}b)>0$ (positive since $H^{-1}\succ 0$ and $b\neq 0$). Hence $$u^*=u_{\mathrm{nom}}+\max\Big\{0,\ \frac{-\psi}{b^\top H^{-1}b}\Big\}H^{-1}b .$$ Geometrically this is the projection of $u_{\mathrm{nom}}$ onto the half-space in the metric $\|v\|_H=\sqrt{v^\top Hv}$: the correction is along $H^{-1}b$, the steepest ascent of $b^\top u$ in that metric, not along $b$. $H=I$ recovers $\mu=-\psi/(b^\top b)$ and the correction $\mu b$. The problem is a strictly convex QP with one affine constraint, so KKT is necessary and sufficient and this is the unique solution.

Numbers: $\psi=-3+1+1=-1$; $H^{-1}b=(1,\tfrac14)$; $b^\top H^{-1}b=1+\tfrac14=\tfrac54$; $\mu=1/(5/4)=0.8$; $u^*=(1,1)+0.8\,(1,\tfrac14)=(1.8,\,1.2)$. Check: $a+b^\top u^*=-3+1.8+1.2=0$, active as expected. With $H=I$ one would get $\mu=0.5$ and $u^*=(1.5,1.5)$: the weighting moved more of the correction into the cheap coordinate.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.3 — An exponential CBF for the double integrator
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Derive the barrier chain and characteristic polynomial, distinguish the two initial-state tests from the input-containing final inequality, and prove invariance for the selected gains by two integrating factors.
exercises.replacement_html:
The barrier is $h=1-p$. Differentiate using the two state equations: $\dot h=-\dot p=-v$ and $\ddot h=-\dot v=-u$. The input first appears in the second derivative, so the relative degree is $2$.

$$\eta_b= egin{bmatrix}1-p\-v\end{bmatrix},\quad F= egin{bmatrix}0&1\0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad G= egin{bmatrix}0\1\end{bmatrix}.$$

With the virtual input $\mu=\ddot h=-u$, the chain equation $\dot\eta_b=F\eta_b+G\mu$ has first row $\dot h=-v$ and second row $ rac{d}{dt}(-v)=-u$. For $K_\alpha=[\kappa_1\ \kappa_2]$, the ECBF constraint is

$$-u\ge-\kappa_1(1-p)+\kappa_2v,\qquad u\le\kappa_1(1-p)-\kappa_2v.$$

The virtual closed-loop matrix is $F-GK_\alpha= egin{bmatrix}0&1\-\kappa_1&-\kappa_2\end{bmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda^2+\kappa_2\lambda+\kappa_1$. Choose real negative poles $-p_1,-p_2$ with positive magnitudes $p_1,p_2$. Matching $(\lambda+p_1)(\lambda+p_2)$ gives $\kappa_1=p_1p_2$ and $\kappa_2=p_1+p_2$, in particular $\kappa_2^2\ge4\kappa_1$.

For the nested construction, $ u_0=h$ and $ u_1=\dot h+p_1h=-v+p_1(1-p)$. The initial-state requirements are $ u_0(x_0)\ge0$ and $ u_1(x_0)\ge0$. At $(p_0,v_0)=(0,1)$, these become $1\ge0$ and $-1+p_1\ge0$, so $p_1\ge1$. These use the positive pole magnitudes: using the negative eigenvalue in $p_1\ge-\dot h(0)/h(0)$ would reverse its intended meaning. If $h(0)=0$, division is unavailable and the test is instead $\dot h(0)\ge0$.

The final nested expression is

$$ u_2=\dot u_1+p_2 u_1=-u-(p_1+p_2)v+p_1p_2(1-p).$$

It contains the input, so $ u_2\ge0$ is the condition to enforce at every time, including the initial instant. It is not an additional condition on the initial state alone. An admissible choice is $p_1=p_2=2$, giving $K_\alpha=[4\ \ 4]$ and

$$u\le4(1-p)-4v.$$

Initially the right side is zero, and the auxiliary initial value is $ u_1(0)=-1+2=1$. With unrestricted input, the constraint is feasible; for instance the equality controller is the linear law $u=4(1-p)-4v$.

To see why the initial tests work, enforce $ u_2\ge0$ along a closed-loop solution. Then $\dot u_1+2 u_1\ge0$, so $(e^{2t} u_1)'\ge0$ and $ u_1(t)\ge u_1(0)e^{-2t}\ge0$. In turn $ u_1=\dot h+2h\ge0$, so $(e^{2t}h)'\ge0$ and $h(t)\ge h(0)e^{-2t}\ge0$. This is the nested HOCBF argument with linear gains $2$, and it proves that the wall is not crossed. Admissible input bounds and existence/regularity of the implemented feedback remain necessary if a different controller is used.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.4 — Input-to-state safety for a bounded disturbance (proof)
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Compute the safeguarding Lie derivatives, solve the destabilizing reciprocal equation and local disturbance range, derive the square-completion inflation, and state its initial-set/existence scope with a full-time bound for the specified nonnegative initial state.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Nominal safety and local disturbance tolerance. Since $h'(x)=-1$, the drift and input derivatives are $L_fh=x$ and $L_gh=-x^2$. With $k=0$, $\dot h=x=2-h\ge-h$. Thus the linear extended class-$\mathcal K$ choice $\alpha(r)=r$ supplies the safeguarding inequality everywhere. The exact undisturbed solution $x(t)=x_0e^{-t}$ also stays at most $2$ whenever $x_0\le2$.

A bounded disturbance can nevertheless defeat this controller. Take $d(t)=1$ and $x_0=2$. Then $\dot x=x^2-x$ is initially $2\gt0$, immediately crossing the boundary. To compute its escape, put $y=1/x$ while $x\gt0$. The chain rule gives $\dot y=-\dot x/x^2=y-1$, with $y(0)=1/2$. Its solution is $y(t)=1-\tfrac12e^t$, hence

$$x(t)=\frac1{1-\tfrac12e^t}\longrightarrow+\infty\quad\text{as }t\uparrow\ln2.$$

This size-one disturbance causes finite-time escape. It does not disprove local ISSf, which only asks for tolerance up to some sufficiently small disturbance bound.

For a local certificate choose $\gamma(r)=r$ and $\bar d=1/4$. Fix $r=\|d\|_\infty\le1/4$. The inflated set is $C_d=\{x\le2+r\}$. At its regular boundary $x=2+r\gt0$, the worst disturbance is $d(t)=r$, and

$$\dot x\le(2+r)\big[-1+r(2+r)\big]\le(2+r)\left(-1+\frac9{16}\right)\lt0.$$

Thus the field points inward at this boundary for every allowed signal; the one-dimensional boundary criterion proves invariance on the solution interval. The function $\gamma(r)=r$ is class $\mathcal K$, so this supplies the requested local ISSf property. More generally, any $\bar d\lt1/2$ allows a sufficiently small positive inflation: choose $\gamma(\bar d)\lt1/\bar d-2$ and an increasing $\gamma$. For $\bar d\ge1/2$, a constant positive disturbance of that size points outward at every upper boundary $2+\gamma(\bar d)\gt2$, so this type of local inflated-set guarantee cannot extend to those bounds.

(b) Add the constructive ISSf correction. The scalar row $L_gh=-x^2$ equals its own transpose, so $k(x)=-x^2$. With $u=-x^2+d(t)$,

$$\dot x=-x-x^4+x^2d(t),\qquad\dot h=x+x^4-x^2d(t).$$

Complete the square in $x^2$:

$$x^4-x^2d=\left(x^2-\frac d2\right)^2-\frac{d^2}{4}\ge-\frac{d^2}{4}.$$

Putting $r=\|d\|_\infty$ gives the requested $\dot h\ge x-r^2/4$. Since $x=2-h$, this also implies $\dot h\ge-h-r^2/4$. Define $\eta=h+r^2/4$, with $r$ a fixed bound on the entire signal. Then $\dot\eta=\dot h\ge-\eta$, and an integrating factor gives $\eta(t)\ge\eta(0)e^{-t}$. Consequently

$$C_d=\left\{x:2-x+\frac{r^2}{4}\ge0\right\}=\left\{x:x\le2+\frac{r^2}{4}\right\}$$

is forward invariant for initial states in $C_d$. Its boundary also satisfies $\dot h\ge0$ and has nonzero gradient $h'=-1$, agreeing with Nagumo's criterion. Starting in the original $C$ therefore gives an upper overshoot allowance $r^2/4$.

As in this module's definition, invariance concerns the maximal interval on which a solution exists. For the specified $x_0=2$, the origin is also an equilibrium of the disturbed equation for every $d(t)$, and uniqueness prevents a trajectory from crossing below zero. The state remains in the compact interval $[0,2+r^2/4]$, so local existence extends to all forward time for bounded measurable $d$. The full upper half-line $C_d$ itself does not supply a compactness or forward-completeness argument for arbitrary negative starts.

(c) Identify the ISSf functions. Use $\alpha(r)=r$, $\iota(r)=r^2/4$, and $\beta(r)=-\alpha(-r)=r$ on $r\ge0$. Thus $\gamma=\beta^{-1}\circ\iota$ is $\gamma(r)=r^2/4$. The extended $\alpha$ and nonnegative-domain $\iota,\gamma$ are increasing and vanish at zero; the latter two are unbounded. The derivative inequality is valid for any finite disturbance level, and the certified inflation tends to zero as that level tends to zero. This compares sets for different signal bounds; the supremum norm of a past-and-future signal does not drop retroactively when its current disturbance becomes zero.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.5 — Discounted safety Bellman equation on three states
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Gives a checked family of distinct undiscounted fixed points, writes all three discounted state equations through four synchronous sweeps, verifies the unique fixed point and safe policy, and computes the geometric error factor.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) $V(F)=\min\{-1,V(F)\}$, $V(B)=\min\{1,\max\{V(A),V(F)\}\}$, $V(A)=\min\{2,\max\{V(A),V(B)\}\}$. Take $V(F)=-1$. Then any $c\in[-1,2]$ with $V(A)=c$, $V(B)=\min\{1,c\}$ is a fixed point: the $B$-equation gives $\min\{1,\max\{c,-1\}\}=\min\{1,c\}$ because $c\ge-1$, and the $A$-equation gives $\min\{2,\max\{c,\min\{1,c\}\}\}=\min\{2,c\}=c$. (For $c\lt-1$ the $B$-equation would force $V(B)=-1\neq c$.) The equation does not pin down $V(A)$ (and even $V(F)=-5$ works), which is the non-contraction problem: value iteration from $V\equiv 0$ stops immediately at $V(A)=0$, wrongly suggesting $A$ has no margin.

(b) $V(x)=\tfrac12 l(x)+\tfrac12\min\{l(x),\max_uV(x^+)\}$. From $V_0\equiv 0$:
sweep 1: $V_1(A)=1+\tfrac12\min\{2,0\}=1$; $V_1(B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\min\{1,0\}=\tfrac12$; $V_1(F)=-\tfrac12+\tfrac12\min\{-1,0\}=-1$.
sweep 2: $V_2(A)=1+\tfrac12\min\{2,\max\{1,\tfrac12\}\}=1.5$; $V_2(B)=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\min\{1,\max\{1,-1\}\}=1$; $V_2(F)=-\tfrac12+\tfrac12(-1)=-1$.
sweep 3: $V_3(A)=1+\tfrac12\min\{2,1.5\}=1.75$; $V_3(B)=1$; $V_3(F)=-1$.
sweep 4: $V_4(A)=1+\tfrac12\cdot 1.75=1.875$; $V_4(B)=1$; $V_4(F)=-1$.

(c) Fixed point: $V(A)=2$ (check: $1+\tfrac12\min\{2,\max\{2,1\}\}=2$), $V(B)=1$, $V(F)=-1$; it is unique by the contraction, and the safe set is $\{V\ge 0\}=\{A,B\}$ with the safe policy "stay at $A$" / "go to $A$". The error $2-V_k(A)$ is $1,\ \tfrac12,\ \tfrac14,\ \tfrac18$: it halves each sweep, the contraction factor $\gamma=\tfrac12$. Note $V(A)=2=l(A)$: discounting did not shrink the value here because the safest action keeps the margin constant; in general $V_\gamma$ interpolates between the current and the future margin.

exercises.label: Exercise 10.6 — Recursive feasibility of the predictive safety filter
exercises.thoroughness_rationale: Construct a feasible plan for every allowed initial state, solve the two optimizations along the actual closed loop, prove the drift example’s finite continuation failure, and distinguish an exact terminal invariant set from a first-order sampled CBF surrogate.
exercises.replacement_html:
(a) Terminal safety and feasible states. At the terminal state $0$, the terminal input $0$ belongs to $U$ and makes the successor $0$. All later states and inputs remain admissible, so Assumption 4.2 holds. The singleton can be represented by the Lipschitz inequality $a_S(x)=1+|x|\le1$.

For every $x\in[-1,1]$, the two-input plan $u_0=u_1=-x/2$ has $|u_i|\le1/2$, intermediate state $x/2\in X$, and terminal state $0$. Hence every state of $X$ is feasible. No initial state outside $X$ is feasible because the problem constrains its initial state as well. The feasible set is exactly $[-1,1]$.

From $x(0)=1$, the terminal equation is $1+u_0+u_1=0$. Both inputs are at least $-1/2$, so their sum can equal $-1$ only if each is $-1/2$. The desired input $u_L=1/2$ is rejected, and the actual first input is $-1/2$, producing $x(1)=1/2$.

At the next step, the unused tail $-1/2$ followed by the terminal input $0$ is a feasible full two-step candidate, producing $0,0$. This proves feasibility, but the filter reoptimizes rather than necessarily using that candidate. At $x=1/2$, write $u_1=-1/2-u_0$. Intersecting both input bounds gives $u_0\in[-1/2,0]$. The objective $|1/2-u_0|$ is smallest at the largest allowed $u_0$, namely $0$. The minimizing plan is therefore $(0,-1/2)$, and its applied first input leaves the current state at $1/2$.

The same optimization repeats at every later step. Thus the realized closed loop is $x(0)=1$, $x(k)=1/2$ for $k\ge1$, with inputs $u(0)=-1/2$, $u(k)=0$ for $k\ge1$. It is safe forever, although it never reaches the terminal set. A planned terminal arrival preserves the option to use a safe continuation; replanning does not commit the plant to execute every planned input.

(b) Why the terminal condition is needed in a less capable plant. For the original integrator, $u=0$ keeps every point of $X$ in $X$. Without a terminal constraint, every $x\in X$ therefore has a safe two-step continuation, and every applied feasible first input leaves another state with that property. This system cannot provide a recursive-feasibility counterexample merely by removing the terminal set.

For the changed plant $x^+=x+u+0.6$, even the strongest negative input leaves a positive increment: $x^+-x\ge-0.5+0.6=0.1$. From $x(0)=0.5$, a feasible plan is $u_0=-0.2$, $u_1=-0.5$, producing states $0.9$ and $1.0$, both in $X$.

These are also the filter's first optimal choices when $u_L=0.5$. To permit a safe second step, the first successor $x_1=1.1+u_0$ must be at most $0.9$, since the second step adds at least $0.1$. Thus $u_0\le-0.2$. Together with $u_0\ge-0.5$, the feasible first-input interval is $[-0.5,-0.2]$; its point closest to $0.5$ is $-0.2$. At the resulting state $0.9$, a new two-step plan is impossible because its final state is at least $0.9+0.1+0.1=1.1$.

The stored one-step tail $-0.5$ still safely reaches $1.0$. At that state every admissible input produces a successor at least $1.1$, so no safe continuation exists. More generally, any admissible sequence satisfies $x(k)\ge x(0)+0.1k$, eventually exceeding $1$. There is no nonempty robust terminal safe set or terminal policy in these bounds. The finite two-step plan is valid for its two steps; it cannot establish indefinite safety without the missing terminal continuation assumption.

(c) A CBF as a one-step continuation certificate. In a horizon-one interpretation, the terminal set is $C=\{h\ge0\}$. An admissible CBF feedback provides a continuation from states in $C$, and the filter restricts its first input to preserve that option. On the first-order sampled model, a CBF inequality gives

$$h(x^+)\ge h(x)-\alpha(h(x))\Delta t.$$

If $h(x)\gt0$ and $\alpha(h(x))\lt h(x)/\Delta t$, this lower bound is positive. At $h(x)=0$, $\alpha(0)=0$ gives the nonnegative boundary value. The one-step successor is therefore again in the terminal set in this approximation, and CBF feasibility there supplies the next candidate input. That is the role analogous to a terminal safe set.

An actual fallback must exist within $U$. For compact $U$, one may select a maximizing barrier-rate input when it satisfies the required bound. For unrestricted inputs and nonzero control coefficient, that affine maximization is unbounded; a feasible minimum-norm input serves instead. Finally, the displayed sampled inequality neglects integration error. An exact held-input guarantee requires a verified intersample error bound or a discrete-time barrier inequality; the clock condition alone does not establish it.
